title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
problem_statement: Optimizing the average loss in multi-task learning frequently causes severe under-optimization of certain tasks due to generalized conflicting gradients, while existing gradient manipulation methods require storing and computing all task gradients at each step, incurring prohibitive O(k) space and time complexities for large models and many-task settings.
domain: Multi-Task Learning — multi-task supervised vision (NYU-v2, CityScapes, CelebA), molecular property prediction on graph neural networks (QM-9), and multi-task reinforcement learning (Meta-World MT10)
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and multiple gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) formulated over task log-loss improvement rates. FAMO maximizes the worst-case instantaneous task loss improvement rate max_{d_t} min_{i} (1/alpha * r_i(alpha, d_t) - 1/2 ||d_t||^2), whose dual problem minimizes 1/2 ||J_t z||^2 over the probability simplex S^k. When the optimal combination weights z* form an interior point, all tasks achieve equal instantaneous loss improvement rates. Continuous-time dynamical system analysis demonstrates that stationary points of FAMO correspond to the minima of the sum of log losses sum_{i=1}^k log l_i(theta).
methodology: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization (FAMO) amortizes the dual optimization across training iterations by performing a single-step gradient descent update on unconstrained task weighting logits xi_t in R^k, where combination weights follow z_t = Softmax(xi_t). The algorithm approximates the gradient of the dual objective without computing individual task gradients by utilizing temporal differences of log losses: delta_t = [nabla^T z_1(xi_t), ..., nabla^T z_k(xi_t)]^T [log l_{1,t} - log l_{1,t+1}, ..., log l_{k,t} - log l_{k,t+1}]^T. Model parameters are updated via theta_{t+1} = theta_t - alpha sum_{i=1}^k (c_t z_{i,t} / l_{i,t}) nabla l_{i,t} through a single backward pass of the weighted loss using re-normalization constant c_t = (sum_{i=1}^k z_{i,t} / l_{i,t})^{-1}. An L2 regularization decay term gamma stabilizes logit updates as an exponential moving average: xi_{t+1} = xi_t - beta (delta_t + gamma xi_t), achieving O(1) space and time complexity per iteration.
datasets: Synthetic 2D two-task optimization problem with five initial parameter points
NYU-v2 — indoor scene dataset comprising 1,449 RGBD images evaluated on 13-class semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal prediction
CityScapes — urban street-view dataset comprising 5,000 RGBD images evaluated on 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation
QM-9 — molecular graph dataset of over 130,000 molecules (110,000 train, 10,000 validation, 10,000 test) evaluated on 11 quantum chemical property regression tasks
CelebA — facial attribute dataset comprising 200,000 images of 10,000 celebrities evaluated on 40 binary facial attribute classification tasks
Meta-World MT10 — multi-task robotic manipulation benchmark comprising 10 distinct manipulation tasks

metrics: Synthetic: 2D loss trajectories, runtime for 50,000 optimization steps, and Pareto front convergence

NYU-v2: Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation; Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation; Mean angle distance, Median angle distance, and percentage within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for surface normals; Mean Rank (MR); average per-task performance drop Delta_m% relative to Single-Task Learning (STL)
QM-9: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) across 11 molecular properties (mu, alpha, HOMO, LUMO, <R^2>, ZPVE, U, U0, H, G, Cv), Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%
CityScapes: mIoU and Pixel Accuracy for semantic segmentation, Absolute Error and Relative Error for depth estimation, Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%
CelebA: Mean classification error across 40 facial attributes, Mean Rank (MR), and Delta_m%
Meta-World MT10: Mean task success rate ± standard error of the mean over 10 random seeds
Computational efficiency: Relative training time per epoch normalized to Linear Scalarization (LS)
baselines: Scale-Invariant Baseline (SI / Sum of Log Losses)
architectures: Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN with SegNet backbone) for NYU-v2 and CityScapes
SchNet graph neural network for QM-9 molecular property prediction
ResNet-18 backbone for CelebA 40-task attribute classification
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) multi-layer perceptron actor-critic network for Meta-World MT10

key_findings: FAMO optimizes multi-task models by decreasing task losses at approximately equal rates using only O(1) space and time per iteration, matching the computational efficiency of standard Adam on the average loss.
On the 2D synthetic benchmark, FAMO resolves conflicting gradients and reaches the Pareto front across all five initializations while training 25 times faster than Nash-MTL.

On NYU-v2 (three tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves Delta_m% = -4.10% and Mean Rank 3.44, outperforming Nash-MTL (-4.04%, MR 2.11), IMTL-G (-0.76%), CAGrad (0.20%), PCGrad (3.97%), and Linear Scalarization (5.59%).

On QM-9 (11 molecular property tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves the best overall Delta_m% = 58.5% and Mean Rank 3.27, outperforming Nash-MTL (62.0%, MR 2.09), IMTL-G (77.2%), Scale-Invariant baseline (77.8%), CAGrad (112.8%), and Linear Scalarization (177.6%).

On CelebA (40 tasks) across three random seeds, FAMO achieves Delta_m% = 4.72% and Mean Rank 1.21, outperforming Nash-MTL (4.97%), CAGrad (6.20%), PCGrad (6.65%), and Linear Scalarization (6.28%), while eliminating the prohibitive O(k) memory overhead of gradient manipulation methods.
On CityScapes (two tasks), FAMO achieves Delta_m% = 8.13% with gamma = 0.01, outperforming CAGrad (11.64%), PCGrad (18.29%), and Linear Scalarization (14.11%).

On the Meta-World MT10 robotic manipulation benchmark over 10 random seeds, FAMO achieves an average success rate of 0.83 ± 0.05, matching CAGrad (0.83 ± 0.05) and exceeding PCGrad (0.72 ± 0.02), Soft Modularization (0.73 ± 0.04), Uncertainty Weighting (0.77 ± 0.05), and shared-model SAC (0.49 ± 0.07).

Training runtime benchmarks demonstrate that FAMO introduces negligible time overhead relative to Linear Scalarization across all task scales, whereas existing gradient manipulation methods scale linearly with the number of tasks k.
scope_and_delimitations: FAMO assumes a shared-parameter multi-task setting where a single input batch allows simultaneous computation of all task losses in a single forward pass.
The method requires smooth non-negative task losses (l_i(theta) >= 0) bounded away from zero by adding a small constant (1e-8) or shifting by known loss lower bounds.

The regularization hyperparameter gamma requires selection from a discrete set {0.0001, 0.001, 0.01} based on validation performance (gamma = 0.01 for CityScapes and gamma = 0.001 for other benchmarks).

The empirical evaluation covers vision, molecular property graphs, and robotic control benchmarks, without evaluating natural language understanding, machine translation, or transformer-based large language models.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: One limitation of FAMO is its dependency on the regularization parameter γ, which is introduced due to the stochastic update of the task weighting logits w. Future work can investigate a more principled way of determining γ.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that FAMO depends on the regularization hyperparameter gamma to stabilize the stochastic updates of the task weighting logits, which currently requires manual hyperparameter tuning. In addition, FAMO assumes that temporal loss differences accurately approximate directional derivatives, which requires small learning rates and smooth loss functions, and can become sensitive when task losses approach zero.

generalizability_gap: The authors did not evaluate FAMO on natural language processing tasks, code-switched or multilingual NLP benchmarks, transformer language models, or multimodal foundation models; furthermore, the method was not evaluated in multi-task scenarios where tasks have unaligned data sources requiring separate forward passes.
methodological_gap: FAMO relies on a first-order Taylor approximation of temporal loss differences to approximate gradient inner products, which can introduce estimation errors under large learning rates or high-variance mini-batch stochasticity. In addition, the regularization decay coefficient gamma must be manually tuned per dataset rather than scheduled dynamically.
future_work: Developing principled and automated methods to dynamically determine or adapt the regularization hyperparameter gamma.
Evaluating FAMO on large language models, multilingual language benchmarks, and multimodal vision-language representations.
Extending FAMO to multi-task learning settings with disjoint datasets that cannot be evaluated in a single forward pass.
Designing adaptive learning rate mechanisms for task weighting logit updates.
